questions.q: Why does Hartwell need an after-action report (AAR) in addition to the risk register update from Lesson 17?
options: The AAR replaces the risk register entirely once an incident is resolved
The register tracks the risk forward in time as a living document, while the AAR is a one-time narrative record of exactly what happened, written for organizational learning
The AAR is only required when a regulator specifically requests it
The register and the AAR contain identical information, so either one alone would be sufficient
questions.explain: The register says what the risk looks like now; the AAR says how this specific incident happened and what it teaches — they serve different purposes and Hartwell needs both.

questions.q: What is the actual root cause of the audit/automation discrepancy, as this lesson states it?
options: Renee Castellano's audit contained a data entry error
Mara's automation double-counted several accounts by mistake
The audit's methodology was scoped to group membership only, and direct ACL grants were never in scope to begin with — a methodology gap, not a data error
The SIEM was misconfigured and logged false privileged-logon events
questions.explain: Both the audit and the automation were internally accurate given what each checked; the gap was in the audit's scope, not in either data source being wrong.

questions.q: What, specifically, is named as 'what went right' in this incident?
options: The March emergency patch was completed on schedule
The automation's dual-check design — group membership, direct grants, and SIEM logon activity together — caught a gap a single-method audit structurally could not
The compliance audit found the discrepancy before the automation did
Hartwell avoided the incident entirely through good luck
questions.explain: The dual-check design was built with exactly this kind of gap in mind back in Lesson 8, and it worked as intended the first time it mattered.

questions.q: What, specifically, is named as 'what went wrong' in this incident?
options: The break-glass grants from the March emergency were never formally revoked once the emergency closed, with no expiry or scheduled sweep to catch them
Break-glass access should never have existed in the first place
Mara's Python automation ran on the wrong schedule
The OT/SCADA segment was never zero-trust at all
questions.explain: The problem wasn't that emergency access existed — it's that nothing enforced the grants' own cleanup once the emergency that justified them had ended.

questions.q: Which corrective action is specifically owned by Renee Castellano, and why does that ownership make sense?
options: Migrating the retained break-glass account to a PAM workflow, because she manages Hartwell's identity platform
Rewriting the quarterly audit query to include direct ACL/IAM grants recursively, because the audit methodology is her process to fix
Formalizing Mara's automation as the standing validation layer, because she wrote the original Python script
Briefing the board, because she is Hartwell's CISO
questions.explain: The audit's methodology gap is Renee's process to correct, since she owns the quarterly privileged-access audit that the new query change applies to.
